newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Rains ease over Ivorian cocoa areas.
newsitem.headline: Rains ease over Ivorian cocoa areas.

text.p: Wet season rains eased in late June after aiding development of Ivory Coast's 1997/98 main cocoa crop (Oct-April), weather and crop analysts said on Monday.
The rains were above normal for June but average for the May to July wet season overall.
"It's good for the main crop," said one crop analyst. "If rains swell the bean size we could also have a good end to the mid-crop (May-Sept)."
Farmers were bringing stocks out to dry along roadsides, suggesting a pick-up in port arrivals during the July-August dry season, he added.
The mid-crop has been slow over the past two months.

Official national weather data for the third 10 days of June show rains averaged 83.2 mm at 10 monitored stations -- down from 147.4 mm in the previous 10 days -- with rains on average falling on five days out of 10.
Data showed cocoa belt rains averaged 350 mm in June but crop analysts point to highly localised heavy rains during the month, which could have skewed data taken from a limited, 10 station sample.
"The rains were well above average but not to that extent," one said, putting the long-term historical figure for June at a little over 200 mm.
An analyst at the national weather centre said, "It (June) was the highest for at least the past 10 years." He did not have an average figure available.

Upcountry cocoa buyers in June pointed to muddy bush tracks making access from plantations to some villages and main roads difficult. The large quantities of mid-crop cocoa in and around villages over the past week suggested cooler and drier early June weather had eased the problem, analysts said.

"We saw good quantities, so you are likely to see a pick-up (of arrivals) in July and August," said one, pointing to June bean sizes of 120-130 beans per 100 grams against an export standard maximum of 105 per 100.
Wet season rains before the 1995/96 crop year continued thoughout July and August, leading to a record 1.2 million tonne harvest.

"Next year (1997/98) should really produce (cocoa)," said one buyer based around Daloa and Gagnoa. "It could be even better than last year," one said, pointing to abundant flowering for cocoa pods in his area.
Next year's crop has been put at anything between just under 900,000 tonnes and 1.1 million tonnes by industry forecasters.
Private forecasters touring plantations said a picture would not emerge until August. They said early indications suggested a big crop.
Port sources said June exports dwindled to 19,050 tonnes, from 27,000 in May. They expected the total of 960,000 since October to rise as drier weather set in.
